head.meta_description: Halal private dining in Dubai: the three questions to ask before you book, how to check a named restaurant yourself, and real per-head prices for every format.
head.h1: Halal Private Dining in Dubai: What to Ask — Real Prices and Timings

opening_paragraph: Halal private dining in Dubai costs AED 700 to 950 per person, and myCHEF arranges the chef who cooks and serves on site. Before you book, confirm three things: that the meat comes from a certified halal supplier, that no pork or cooking alcohol is used, and that the kitchen keeps ingredients separate.

The worry underneath that search is finding out afterwards that the food was not what you were told it was, in front of guests who trusted you to check. A good chef answers all three questions up front and adapts any cuisine to suit. This guide, updated for 2026, covers what to ask, how to run the same check on a restaurant you found for yourself, and what each format costs per head.

replace_in_block.new_heading: What halal private dining in Dubai means
new_paragraphs: Halal private dining means a professional chef cooks a full menu in your home, villa or venue to halal standards from start to finish. That covers more than the meat. It means no pork anywhere in the service, no wine or spirits in sauces and reductions, and real care to keep compliant ingredients away from anything that is not. A booking usually includes menu design around your tastes, fresh shopping, cooking on site, plated or family-style service, and a full clean-down before the chef leaves. You keep your own kitchen while the chef brings the skill and the discipline. Because everything is prepared in front of you instead of trucked in from an unseen kitchen, halal private dining explained this way is one of the quickest ways to be sure how your food was handled.

replace_in_block.new_heading: How much does halal private dining cost in Dubai?
new_paragraphs: Halal private dining in Dubai starts from about AED 700 per person, with most bookings between AED 700 and AED 950 per person depending on cuisine, courses and guest count. There is no halal premium; the cost reflects the menu and the chef, not the dietary standard. If you prefer fixed prices, set packages run from AED 1,200 for a compact dinner up to AED 5,500 for an elaborate multi-course event, with popular tiers around AED 2,400, AED 3,600 and AED 4,500 in between. A dedicated tasting menu is about AED 1,400. Prices usually cover the chef, menu planning and cooking on site, while premium ingredients such as prime cuts or seafood are quoted on top. Ask for an itemised proposal so the cost is clear before you commit.
The per-head rate moves with guest count, because a chef's evening costs roughly the same whether they cook for two or for twenty. These are the published bands:
Private chef, cooked and served on site — per person, before 5% VAT Guests Per person

Romantic private dining in Dubai is the smallest version of this and, as the table shows, the most expensive per head — a dinner for two lands at AED 950 to 1,300 per person, because you are buying a chef's whole evening instead of a share of one. There is no minimum headcount on the plated service; a table for two is a real booking, not an exception we make.

If you are searching for affordable private dining in Dubai and those figures sit above what you had in mind, say so when you enquire, because the honest answer is a different format, not a quietly thinned-out chef. Catered formats start from AED 90 per head for a working lunch, AED 120 for a standard event buffet, and AED 150 for a premium buffet, BBQ or canapés, with a minimum of 10 guests, 20 for a buffet, and a minimum order of AED 900. Those are food formats — delivered or set up for you — not a chef cooking and serving at your table, and the distance between AED 150 and AED 700 is precisely that difference in labour, not a difference in the halal standard. Both are held to the same sourcing questions above.
What is the short answer?

Before you book halal private dining in Dubai, ask the chef to confirm the meat is sourced from a certified halal supplier, that there is no pork and no cooking alcohol, whether the kitchen keeps ingredients separate, and how everything is verified.
How much does halal private dining in Dubai cost?

It starts from about AED 700 per person, with most events between AED 700 and AED 950 per person. Fixed packages run from AED 1,200 to AED 5,500, and a tasting menu is around AED 1,400. There is no halal premium.
How is halal certified in the UAE?

UAE halal certification is regulated by the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology, formerly ESMA, under the national standard UAE.S 2055. The National Halal Mark shows a supply chain checked against those rules. For a private dinner, ask that meat and poultry come from certified halal suppliers.
Is a private chef halal by default?

Not automatically. A private chef is halal when they source certified meat, use no pork or cooking alcohol, and keep ingredients separate. Any chef used to Muslim households does this as standard, so confirm it when you enquire.
Which cuisines can be cooked halal?

Almost all of them. Arabic and Indian are natural fits, but Italian, Mediterranean, Pan-Asian and fine dining menus all work halal with the right sourcing. The style of food is not the limit; the sourcing and preparation are.
Is No5 Dining halal? Is Social Hideout halal?

We do not publish other venues' halal status, because sourcing and licences change and a second-hand answer can be out of date without anyone noticing. Call the venue and ask three things: is all the meat and poultry from a certified halal supplier, is any wine, beer or spirit used in the cooking, and can you send the current certificate. The same three questions settle any named place, including whether a particular G private dining room or restaurant meets your standard.
Is Dove halal?

It depends on the specific product and on the country you bought it in. A brand cleared by one authority for one market is not automatically cleared for another, and confectionery and personal-care ranges sold under the same name are assessed separately. Check the certification mark on the pack itself and the manufacturer's published certificate for your market.
Do you have a halal private dining room, or a cafe with a private room in Dubai?

No. MyCHEF does not operate a restaurant or a private room of its own, so if you want one of the restaurants with private cabins in Dubai, book with the venue directly. What we do instead is send a vetted chef to cook in your home, villa, yacht or office, which is why the sourcing questions on this page are answerable in your own kitchen.
What is the most affordable way to do this?

Change the format, not the standard. A plated private chef is AED 700 to 950 per person at ten guests. Catered formats start from AED 90 per head for a working lunch, AED 120 for an event buffet and AED 150 for a premium buffet, BBQ or canapés, with a 10-guest minimum, 20 for a buffet, and a minimum order of AED 900. The halal sourcing is identical; the service is not.
How far ahead should I book, and can you cater near me?

Book a few weeks ahead for busy dates like Ramadan, New Year and wedding season, though shorter notice is often possible. MyCHEF covers homes and venues across Dubai, so a halal private chef near you can usually be arranged wherever you are hosting.
How do I get an exact quote?
Share your date, guest count and venue with myCHEF and you will get an itemised proposal, usually within one business day.

add_block.new_heading: The questions to ask a caterer: your halal checklist
new_paragraphs: Three questions do most of the work, and together they make a simple pre-booking checklist. First, is the meat and poultry sourced from a certified halal supplier? Second, is any pork or alcohol used anywhere in the cooking, including stocks, marinades and desserts? Third, how is the kitchen kept separate from non-compliant ingredients, boards and oil? A few practical tips sharpen it further: ask the chef to name their suppliers, to explain how they handle a mixed guest list with allergies, and what happens if a guest asks to see certification on the day. Clear, specific answers show a chef takes halal private dining seriously. Vague ones tell you to keep looking. Asking out loud reveals more in two minutes than any brochure.

add_block.new_heading: How is halal certified in the UAE?
new_paragraphs: Halal food in the UAE sits inside a real regulatory framework, not just a label on a menu. Certification is overseen by the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology, formerly ESMA, and the national standard UAE.S 2055 sets the general requirements a product must meet to be called halal. The National Halal Mark, a red crescent with the word "halal" in Arabic and English, signals a supply chain that has been checked against those rules. For a private dinner you are not buying a boxed certified product, so the practical version is simpler: your chef should buy meat and poultry from certified halal suppliers and be able to tell you who they are. That standard is what sits behind every question in this checklist.

add_block.new_heading: “Is No5 Dining halal?” — a worked example you can repeat for any venue in five minutes
new_paragraphs: Some of the most-asked questions in this whole topic are about one specific place. Is No5 Dining halal. Is Social Hideout halal. Is G private dining halal. We are not going to answer those for you, and you should be careful with any site that does. Sourcing changes when a supplier changes, an alcohol licence can be added or dropped, and a stranger repeating what was true eighteen months ago is exactly how people end up eating something they did not intend to. What we can hand you is the check itself, and it takes about five minutes on the phone.

Call the venue instead of emailing, and ask three things in this order. First: is all the meat and poultry from a certified halal supplier, or only part of the menu? Plenty of places in Dubai serve halal meat and still hold an alcohol licence, so “we are halal” and “we serve no alcohol” are two separate claims and you may care about both. Second: is wine, beer or spirits used anywhere in the cooking — sauces, reductions, marinades, desserts? Third: can you send me the certificate, and is it current? A kitchen that is sure of its sourcing answers all three without pausing and is happy to put it in writing. An answer that quietly narrows to “the chicken is”, or a promise to check and call back that does not arrive, is also an answer.

The same logic covers packaged brands, which is why a question like “is Dove halal” turns up alongside restaurant searches. It depends on the product and on the country: a brand cleared by one authority for one market is not automatically cleared for another, and confectionery and personal-care lines sold under the same name are assessed separately. Read the certification mark on the pack in front of you and check the manufacturer's published certificate for the market you bought it in, instead of a forum thread about a different country's supply chain.

add_block.new_heading: A private room at a restaurant, or a chef at your own table?
new_paragraphs: A lot of people who search for halal private dining want a venue — a cafe with a private room in Dubai, one of the restaurants with private cabins in Dubai, or one of the Indian restaurants with private dining that will hold a back room for a family dinner. That is a different product from ours and it is fairer to say so plainly. MyCHEF does not run a restaurant and has no halal private dining room of its own to book. We send a chef to your home, villa, yacht or office, and the cooking happens where you are.

Three things usually decide which one suits you. Privacy is the first: a private room or cabin is a partitioned part of a working restaurant, so you still share the building, the service rhythm and the kitchen with the other tables, whereas at home the only people in the room are yours. Control over sourcing is the second, and it is the reason this page exists — in your own kitchen you can see the packaging the meat came in, which no amount of asking at a venue can match. Cost is the third, and it does not fall the way most people expect: halal dine-in restaurants with a private room often charge a room hire or a minimum spend on top of the food, and once you add that up the gap to a private chef is smaller than the menu prices suggest.

If a room at a venue is still what you want, book it directly with the venue and run the three questions above before you pay a deposit. A private cabin does not change the kitchen your dinner comes out of.

add_block.new_heading: Halal private dining menu ideas across cuisines
new_paragraphs: Almost any cuisine can be cooked to halal standards, so your menu ideas are not limited to one style. Arabic and Indian menus suit it naturally, but Italian, Mediterranean, Pan-Asian and modern fine dining all work with the right sourcing. The difference is certified meat and no cooking alcohol, not the flavour. Popular choices include a mezze-led Arabic spread, a Levantine grill, a Mughlai feast, or a multi-course tasting that travels through several cuisines. Vegetarian, vegan and pescatarian courses are halal by nature and slot in easily. The best menus are planned around your guests, so when you review a proposal, ask where the meat comes from and how any wine-based sauce or alcohol-based dessert extract is replaced.

add_block.new_heading: Halal private dining for Ramadan iftar and suhoor
new_paragraphs: Ramadan is when halal private dining is booked most, and the dates matter. The UAE set Ramadan 2026 to begin on 18 February , which means iftar and suhoor bookings fill up weeks ahead. According to the UAE Government , the holy month has two main meals: suhoor before dawn and iftar to break the fast at sunset, and the fast is traditionally opened with dates. A private chef lets you host either at home, with a menu that moves from dates and soups through grilled mains to Arabic sweets. Layla Hassan, whose cooking is built around Arabic and Ramadan menus, is the chef we usually match for these evenings.

add_block.new_heading: Why Ramadan changes the questions you ask
new_paragraphs: Halal sourcing is a year-round standard, but Ramadan changes the service around it. Private-sector working hours reduce by 2 daily during Ramadan under UAE labour rules ( UAE government portal ), which compresses the working day and pushes hospitality into the evening. Iftar is timed to sunset instead of to a convenient hour, so the kitchen works to a fixed external clock.

That has two practical consequences worth raising when you book. First, ask how the chef handles a hard start time instead of a service window, because everything must be ready at once. Second, ask about staffing: the same evening hours are in demand across the city for the whole month, so confirm the team is committed to your date instead of provisionally held.

add_block.new_heading: The Food Code sits behind the halal question
new_paragraphs: Halal sourcing answers what the food is; the Food Code answers how it is handled. Dubai Municipality publishes the Dubai Food Code alongside food-establishment requirements by activity, a mandatory integrated training system for food establishments, and separate rules for food transportation and delivery vehicles. Those apply to the kitchen your halal menu comes from regardless of the sourcing standard.

So ask both questions instead of one. Where does the meat come from, and who holds the food-safety training for the kitchen preparing it? For a private dinner at home the transport rules matter especially, because the food travels to you: ask how it is packed, how long it is in transit and how it is held on arrival.
